summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that patchwork, but the same report warns that formal availability of a procedure does not guarantee smooth implementation.

Violence risk in the state is documented. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 July 2023 that Brayan Rivera was presented before a US judge for extradition, accused by Mexican authorities of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in a Tijuana hotel in the tolerance zone; the Baja California attorney general described him as a serial perpetrator and said the investigation linked him to at least three feminicides. Zeta Tijuana further reported on 8 March 2025 that 1,179 women have been killed in the state under the current governor while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide, indicating systematic under-classification of lethal violence against women.

Impunity is the national backdrop. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that over 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide on 18 July 2024 under the Paola Buenrostro law with sentences of up to 70 years. Baja California has not enacted an equivalent transfemicide statute.

Same-sex marriage has been legal nationally since 2009, so partnership recognition is settled for visitors to Baja California.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) on Tabasco provides a baseline for how a non-reforming Mexican state behaves: no recognition procedure, institutional mistreatment of trans people, an unsolved August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez, no hate-motivation provisions in the criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely outting patients by using legal names. Baja California's reformed position contrasts with that pattern, though the same national enforcement gap identified by Caroline Beer's LSE USAPP analysis (22 November 2024) applies: progressive legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice.

Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged Mexican federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Female economic participation in Baja California stood at roughly 46-47%, ranking 14th of 32 states, a general indicator of women's standing in the state.
localsOnly:
Residents of Baja California can use the state's administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, which since the 2024 Civil Code reform covers adults, individuals under 18, and non-binary people. The 2022 original procedure applied only to adults until the Supreme Court invalidated that limitation in June 2023.

Residents face the state's documented under-classification of lethal violence against women: 1,179 women killed under the current governor with only 110 cases typified as feminicide, per Zeta Tijuana (8 March 2025). The state attorney general's office has pursued serial-feminicide suspects through US extradition channels, as in the Brayan Rivera matter, but extradition timelines were stated as ranging from 15 days to two years.

Baja California has not adopted a transfemicide statute comparable to Mexico City's Paola Buenrostro law of 18 July 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve how Baja California's recognition procedure is administered in practice: processing times, fees, documentation requirements, and whether officials apply the under-18 and non-binary provisions consistently are not sourced here.

No Baja California-specific data on hate-crime charging, police treatment of trans complainants, or access to gender-affirming healthcare appears in the inventory; the Tabasco healthcare-outing finding is a comparator from another state, not a Baja California finding.

The Zeta Tijuana feminicide cases cited involve cisgender women victims; whether any of the linked killings targeted trans victims is not stated in the sources.
